physical_painpoints: Product breaks or malfunctions during routine use
Material quality is inferior to what was advertised
Key features stop working at critical moments
emotional_painpoints: Feeling betrayed and foolish after purchase
Anger and helplessness when a main feature fails
Frustration from wasted time and money
Sense of being exploited when high price meets low trust
use_case_disasters: A daily carry item snaps under normal load
A kitchen gadget stops working after a few uses
A tool fails during a simple, routine task
evidence_quotes: I thought it looked good online, but it fell apart in a week.
They show it in perfect settings, but it can't handle real life.
I just want something that works without me having to worry.

strategy.core_pain: Feels deceived by polished marketing that promises aspirational quality but delivers flimsy, unreliable products that fail in real-world use.
evidence_basis: Profile trust_barriers: Skepticism of marketing claims, need for proof of durability beyond lifestyle photos, requirement for transparent manufacturing and accountability.
Profile anxiety_points: Marketing images do not match real-world performance.
Profile painpoint quotes: 'They show it in perfect settings, but it can't handle real life.'
Profile painpoint.use_case_disasters: specific failure scenarios like daily carry load, kitchen gadget after 100 uses, tool during routine task.
Profile dopamine.relief_moment: 'When the product survives a real-world stress test...'
Profile dopamine.viral_emotion: 'Relief and vindication—sharing the story of a product that exceeded expectations and restored trust.'
Profile dopamine.contrast_mechanism: contrast between polished presentation and actual performance.
strategy.identity_attack: You are not a lifestyle influencer. You are someone who needs tools that work when life gets messy. Stop buying products that are built for photoshoots instead of your actual Tuesday.
strategy.status_desire: To be seen as a practical, no-nonsense person who makes smart, durable choices—not someone fooled by flashy ads.
strategy.future_self_gap: Current self: frustrated, skeptical, burned by past purchases. Future self: vindicated, confident, a savvy owner of gear that delivers on its promises.
strategy.broken_expectation: The product's marketing promised aspirational quality and lifestyle perfection, but the actual experience was flimsy and unreliable, creating a negative contrast with reality.
strategy.visual_hook: Raw, single-camera stress test video: a product undergoing repetitive real-world abuse (e.g., 100 uses, a drop, a spill) with a timer and no music—showing either survival or failure.
emotional_arc: Frustration: 'I've been burned by marketing before.'
Skepticism: 'This looks too good to be true.'
Relief: 'Finally, a product that survives my actual life.'
Vindication: 'I made the right choice—and I want to tell others.'
strategy.trust_barrier: Skepticism of marketing claims and need for proof of durability beyond lifestyle photos, requiring transparent manufacturing and accountability.
strategy.objection_handling: Address the 'flimsy after a week' fear head-on with transparent materials & warranty section: 'This hinge is rated for 10,000 cycles. Here is the test report. If it fails in the first year, we replace it, no questions asked.'
strategy.conversion_mechanism: Replace aspirational hero image with side-by-side 'What you see in ads vs. What you get in your hands' comparison, plus transparent materials & warranty section that directly addresses anxiety points.
strategy.cta_logic: Click to see the stress test video or view the materials report—not to 'buy now.' Conversion happens after trust is proven through raw evidence.
risk_notes: Product evidence confidence is 0.45—the product's actual durability is unproven; strategy relies on engineering data that may not exist.
Stress test videos may backfire if the product fails in tests; must be based on real failure rates.
Vindication Loop requires a high-tolerance warranty policy that is a cost center; needs financial modeling to ensure lifetime value exceeds replacement costs.
Review data is mock (data_warnings), so specific failure modes are illustrative, not proven; strategy must be validated with real customer feedback.
If stress test videos have low engagement after 30 days, pivot to 'transparent honesty' strategy acknowledging first-version flaws.

scenes.scene_goal: Hook attention with visceral failure trigger
scenes.visual_description: Single camera, handheld. A kitchen counter. A cheap-looking kitchen gadget (e.g., a garlic press or vegetable chopper) sits next to a timer. The timer reads 'USE #47.' The gadget is visibly bent, plastic deformed.
scenes.narration: Day 47 with the 'premium' gadget they showed in the ad.
scenes.retention_reason: The crack sound and timer trigger flimsy anxiety

scenes.visual_description: Split screen. Left side: The same broken gadget, now in a trash can. Right side: A slow, steady shot of a heavy-duty metal tool (e.g., a ratcheting wrench or a cast-iron skillet) being used to crush a walnut. No music. Just the sound of the crack.
scenes.narration: They sold you a photoshoot. You needed a Tuesday.
scenes.retention_reason: Split screen visually reinforces marketing vs reality

scenes.scene_goal: Provide evidence to overcome trust barrier
scenes.visual_description: Close-up of the metal tool's hinge. A timestamp appears: 'TEST: 10,000 CYCLES.' The tool is opened and closed rapidly, 10 times in 2 seconds. Then a cut to a PDF document on a phone screen: 'MATERIALS REPORT: 6061 Aluminum. Heat-treated. Tensile strength: 310 MPa.'
scenes.narration: This hinge? Rated for ten thousand cycles. Here's the test report. If it fails in the first year, we replace it. No questions.
scenes.retention_reason: Test report and warranty directly address trust barrier

scenes.visual_description: A person's hand, dirty, using the same metal tool to tighten a bolt on a bicycle. The tool doesn't slip. The person exhales, a small, satisfied sound.
scenes.narration: It doesn't need to look good in a magazine. It just needs to work when you need it.
scenes.retention_reason: Real context usage provides emotional relief

scenes.visual_description: The same hand, now holding the tool, points the camera at a small, worn-out sticker on the tool's handle: 'MADE IN USA' or 'LIFETIME WARRANTY.' The camera pulls back to show the person's face—a normal person, not a model—smiling slightly, nodding.
scenes.narration: I stopped buying gear for influencers. I bought gear for me.

scenes.scene_goal: Drive low-barrier CTA with trust-first logic
scenes.visual_description: A simple, static screen. No music. Two buttons: LEFT BUTTON: 'WATCH THE STRESS TEST (RAW, NO MUSIC)' RIGHT BUTTON: 'VIEW MATERIALS REPORT & WARRANTY'
scenes.narration: Don't buy it yet. Watch it break first. Then decide.
scenes.retention_reason: CTA lowers barrier by delaying purchase until trust proven
scenes.linked_painpoint: purchase hesitation from lack of evidence
